# When One Life Has Ended and the Next Hasn’t Begun

Your little one can get really loud in the gap after one life ends and before the next one has formed. A breakup will do it, or moving to another country, an illness, losing your faith or a role, your youngest moving out. So can leaving a family or community, or staying in one on new terms. Tibetan Buddhism calls an in-between state a bardo. You don't have to buy what it teaches about death and rebirth to use the everyday part: endings leave a stretch where the old you is gone and the new one hasn't shown up.

Ask what has ended, and what you're still trying to keep going. What isn't known yet? What is your little one afraid will happen in the gap? Maybe a practical act or small ritual could mark the ending: "This part is over, and I don't know what comes next." When that not-knowing feels unbearable, it's tempting to grab some new identity just so it stops. Don't force one. The grown-up you can keep your routines and protect your body. Grieving what ended is part of it, and so is staying with your little one while the next life takes shape.

Missing someone doesn't have to turn into one more problem to solve. Sometimes the ache itself can be a cue for love, so don't push it away. If love is there, let "I miss you" become "I love you," or a simple wish: "May you be safe. May you be held in love." Picture them, or just feel yourself sending it their way. Does any of it reach them? You don't have to believe it does, since this is about what happens in you. It doesn't replace grieving or getting in touch. You'd still keep your boundaries and do whatever practical things need doing. If sending love makes you more compulsive or unreal, make it simpler: "I miss you, and I care." Same if you can't get back to your life afterward. You can also offer some of the same care to the part of you that's still here.

t65z_seclm4w1:
## How Much Happiness Do You Know Is Possible?

Part of love is wanting someone to be well, and how far that wish can reach depends partly on what kind of happiness you know is possible. If the happiness you know is food, safety, affection, friends, work that means something and some help when you need it, then wanting those things for somebody is love. Babies get some of this already. Practical love matters a lot.

But a big spiritual experience can show you a kind of peace, or a love, you didn't know existed, and then "I want you to be happy" suddenly means something much bigger. That's partly why loving-kindness meditation can sound almost comically simple to someone who's never been near what it's pointing at, and so powerful to someone who has. Saying "may you be happy" over and over isn't automatically some profound love. It's one way of finding that deeper love and growing it.

If you're curious about that bigger happiness, follow the curiosity instead of pretending to believe something. Read people from different traditions, and judge a path by its fruits (what it does for the people on it). Meet people whose lives make you wonder, the kind you walk away from thinking, "Where does that come from?"

Sometimes care isn't what's missing. A meal or a boundary can still help, and so can a kind sentence. But when the whole horizon of life feels too small, none of that touches the question underneath: "Why should I want this life at all?" You might not have put it in those words. Take that question seriously, though. If being alive feels like something you just endure, what would have to be possible for it to feel worth discovering?

Curiosity can be enough here, something like "Other people say they've felt a depth of love or peace that I never have. I don't know if I believe their explanation. But what if the experience is possible for me?" Don't assume the limits of what you've felt so far are the limits of what's possible.

## How Much Happiness Do You Know Is Possible?

Part of love is wanting someone to be well, and how far that wish can reach depends partly on what kind of happiness you know is possible. If the happiness you know is food, safety, affection, friends, work that means something and some help when you need it, then wanting those things for somebody is love. Babies get some of this already. Practical love matters a lot.

But a big spiritual experience can show you a kind of peace, or a love, you didn't know existed, and then "I want you to be happy" suddenly means something much bigger. That's partly why loving-kindness meditation can sound almost comically simple to someone who's never been near what it's pointing at, and so powerful to someone who has. Saying "may you be happy" over and over isn't automatically some profound love. It's one way of finding that deeper love and growing it.

If you're curious about that bigger happiness, follow the curiosity instead of pretending to believe something. Read people from different traditions, and meet people whose lives make you wonder. You might already know someone like that, who's happy in a way you can't quite figure out. And judge a path by its fruits: what are the people who follow it like?

Sometimes the whole horizon of life feels too small. Care isn't what's missing then. A meal can help, or a boundary, or a kind sentence, without touching the question underneath: "Why should I want this life at all?" Take that question seriously. Maybe right now, life is something you're just enduring. What would have to be possible for being alive to feel worth discovering?

Curiosity can be enough here, something like "Other people say they've felt a depth of love or peace that I never have. I don't know if I believe their explanation. But what if the experience is possible for me?" Don't assume the limits of what you've felt so far are the limits of what's possible.

# When the Practice Feels Real but Stays Shallow

Some people have the opposite problem. It feels like you're connecting with your little one, but the contact is staying near the surface. Meditating for a long time and then sleeping can open up much more emotionally direct stuff, especially in a second sleep, after you've already slept once. If that night's dream carries far more feeling and need than the daytime session came anywhere near, you might wake up wondering where all that was. That gap is the sign, and the difference is information about the session (a good session that just didn't carry into your day is something else). Ask what became available, and how you see it now. If repeated nightmares start wrecking your sleep, change the dose before giving up on the whole thing. Try it earlier in the day, or shorter.

## Journal With Each Hand

This is for when talking to your little one, or picturing them, only gets you silence. Write the scared or hurting thoughts and feelings with the hand you don't usually write with (the clumsy one). Its writing already looks like a child's, so that's your little one's hand. Then answer with your usual hand, as the grown-up offering love, protection and guidance. If your little one is still silent, it's tempting to make up what they'd say. But write only what's really there, what you actually feel. The protective part might show up first. Then let it have the clumsy hand until it's said its piece.

If thinking things through on paper leaves you more confused, a simpler memory aid is fine. It keeps track of things without you having to work out what they mean at the same time. Looking for patterns can come later, if it's useful at all. A memory aid doesn't have to explain your life. It could be a short note of what happened, with the date, or a note of what helped. A reminder or a next step works too. Or you can leave yourself a voice note.

## “And So That’s the Way It Happened!”

Finish a hard memory with "And so that's the way it happened!" the way a grandpa would finish a story on the porch. ("Once upon a time…" helps if the start is where you get stuck.) Somehow it moves the whole thing out of the courtroom, where the case was still being argued, and into your life story. Pick a memory you can handle for the first few tries.

Telling it as a story doesn't make it fiction, or prove every detail is right. It ends the trial. Whoever did the harm is still accountable: if it was you, any repair that's owed is still owed, and if someone hurt you, the line doesn't say what they did was okay. Stop if the grandpa voice starts sneering or the shame gets bigger. Same if you start to feel unreal. You might think, "I'll just tell it from further away, then." More distance won't help with those. If the line helps, keep it to just that. Then you can ask what the younger you in that story needs from you now.

## One Intention in the Morning, One Review at Night

In the morning, pick one small intention: "Today I will notice one hook before I act from it." You don't have to know yet which hook it'll be. Whichever one shows up will do. At night, look back over the day without putting yourself on trial. Where did you notice the hook? And where did it run its whole course anyway?

Maybe you only catch it now, looking back: "Oh, I got hooked there." That's still noticing, and it counts as progress. If you interrupted the pattern somewhere, notice that too. What comes next, a small repair or some way to protect yourself? And what moment did you actually get that felt warm, or that you enjoyed? It might have been a time you were brave, or felt close to someone. Repair whatever can be repaired. Then renew the intention and go to sleep.

## One Intention in the Morning, One Review at Night

In the morning, choose one modest intention: "Today I will notice one hook before I act from it." Any hook will do, whichever one shows up. At night, go back over the day without putting yourself on trial (yes, that courtroom again). Where did you notice the hook? Where did it run its whole sequence anyway? Some days those turn out to be the same place.

Noticing counts as progress, even if it's only now, looking back, that you think "oh, that was a hook." If you interrupted the pattern somewhere, notice that too. What's the next small repair, or something protective you can do? And what moment of warmth or pleasure did you actually get? Or it might have been a moment of courage, or of connection. Repair what can be repaired and renew the intention, and then go to sleep.

## Just Like Me

This one works best on a steadier day, when thinking about other people won't pull you out of your own shoes. Name the feeling plainly. Lonely, say. Then think of how many people are feeling that exact thing right now, and wanting it to stop, just like you. Some of them make it worse trying to get away from it. Just like you, sometimes. 😅 Wish all of you, you first, enough support to stay with it, so the pain stops with you.

Breathe however you normally do, and after you, the wish takes in anyone else who comes to mind. The idea is you stop carrying a feeling this many people share as proof that you alone are defective. If one of them hurt you, you might wonder if you're supposed to forgive them, or imagine their childhood. It isn't asking you to. You don't contact anyone for this, either. Whether you ever contact them is a separate decision, and never one to make while you're flooded.

t65z_secsp9w1:
## Close the Session and Return to Life

Give every session with your little one a definite ending. Look around and name where you are, and feel your feet or the chair, wherever you're touching something. Let your jaw and hands relax. They might have been tight this whole time. Then name one normal thing you'll do next and say something like, "That's enough for today. We're returning to the life we're building." Maybe it doesn't feel like enough. Going back to your life is part of the healing, too, and the session doesn't have to resolve every feeling before you make food or go to sleep.

## Close the Session and Return to Life

Every session with your little one needs a definite ending, photo or not. Look around and name where you are. Feel where you're touching something, like the floor under your feet or the chair, and relax your jaw and hands.
